templates.name: Main idea, informational study report (incl. explainer and scholar-argument passages)

items.passage: On degraded Mediterranean terrain, the shrub Ephedra fragilis is frequently among the earliest colonizers of open ground, where it subsequently functions as a nurse plant, sheltering the seedlings of other species. On Dragonera, an islet off the coast of Mallorca, Constanza Neghme and colleagues determined that the lizard Podarcis lilfordi, the shrub’s only known seed disperser there, deposits most of the seeds it consumes in such exposed locations. Seeds that simply dropped beneath a parent shrub experienced greater predation, and none of the resulting seedlings survived the study period.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about Podarcis lilfordi on Dragonera?
options: It likely lowers the number of Ephedra fragilis seedlings that survive on the islet, since it carries seeds away from the parent shrubs.
Its disappearance from the islet would likely make it harder for new plants of other species to grow in open areas.
It likely spreads the seeds of the plants that grow in the shelter of Ephedra fragilis as well as the seeds of the shrub itself.
It likely relies on Ephedra fragilis shrubs for cover when it crosses open ground, much as the seedlings of other species do.
items.explanation: The lizard is the shrub’s “only known seed disperser there” and leaves most seeds in “exposed locations,” while seeds that “dropped beneath a parent shrub” yielded no seedlings that “survived the study period.” So new Ephedra fragilis shrubs in open ground depend on the lizard. Because the shrub shelters “the seedlings of other species” there, losing the lizard would likely make it harder for other plants to grow in open areas too.

A.why_wrong: The lizard does carry seeds away from parent shrubs, but seeds left beneath parents produced no surviving seedlings, so moving them raises survival rather than lowering it.

C.recipe: plausible but unsupported (extends the lizard's role)
C.why_wrong: The text says only that the lizard disperses Ephedra fragilis seeds; it never says the lizard eats or spreads the seeds of the plants the shrub shelters.

D.recipe: twisted detail (sheltering role moved to the lizard)
D.why_wrong: The shrub is said to shelter the seedlings of other plant species; nothing in the text says the lizard uses the shrubs for cover.

sources.what: Neghme, Santamaria and Calvino-Cancela 2017, PLoS ONE: on Dragonera islet (off NW Mallorca) Podarcis lilfordi is the only known seed disperser of the pioneer shrub Ephedra fragilis; dispersal mostly to open sites; undispersed seeds under mother plants suffered higher predation and no seedlings from them survived the study period; the shrub establishes in open ground on degraded lands and acts as a nurse plant for other species

items.notes: Natural science (ecology). Chain: lizard is the only disperser and moves seeds to open ground, where the shrub's new plants come from; the shrub then shelters other species' seedlings; unstated conclusion: losing the lizard would hurt other species' establishment in the open. Left out: the shrub can also spread vegetatively (the key is hedged with likely). Band 6: each distractor keeps a passage fact and fails on the link drawn from it.

fixes: first author named as the paper's byline gives her (Constanza Neghme, not Celedon-Neghme)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PLoS ONE abstract and full text (PMC5565188): sole known disperser, dispersal to open sites, no seedlings from undispersed seeds survived, nurse plants on degraded land.

band7.why: Three-link chain (sole disperser, recruitment only in the open, nurse role) to an unstated consequence; A reverses the effect of a true detail, C and D extend the lizard's role from passage nouns; key hedged and paraphrased. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: An insect struck by a sideways gust can reorient itself actively, by modifying its wing movements, or passively, through aerodynamic forces that its ordinary wingbeat generates. Most flying insects beat their wings in a stroke that rises higher above the body than it descends below it, an asymmetry known as positive stroke dihedral. Using computational simulations of fruit flies and test flights of flapping-wing robots engineered with the same asymmetry, Diana Olejnik and colleagues demonstrated that the asymmetry by itself rotates a flier toward a sideways gust.
items.stem: What does the text most strongly suggest about the wingbeats of most flying insects?
options: They likely help insects sense the direction of a sideways gust, so that the insects can then change how they move their wings to face it.
They likely steady fruit flies in sideways gusts more reliably than they steady the flapping-wing robots that imitate the flies’ asymmetry.
They likely protect insects from sideways gusts mainly by limiting how far the insects tip over toward one side.
They likely allow many insects to turn into a sideways gust without changing the way they beat their wings.
items.explanation: The text says that “most flying insects” have “positive stroke dihedral” and that this asymmetry “by itself rotates a flier toward a sideways gust.” A turn produced this way is passive: it comes from “aerodynamic forces that its ordinary wingbeat generates,” not from “modifying its wing movements.” So most insects can likely turn into a gust without altering their wingbeat.

A.why_wrong: Insects do turn to face gusts, but the asymmetry turns a flier toward the gust “by itself,” which is the passive route, not a cue for the insect to change its wing movements.

B.why_wrong: The researchers found the same turning effect in simulated flies and in robots; the text never compares how reliably the asymmetry works in each.

C.why_wrong: The text describes the asymmetry turning a flier toward the gust; it says nothing about keeping insects from tipping to one side.

sources.what: Olejnik, Muijres, Karasek, Honfi Camilo, De Wagter and de Croon 2022, Frontiers in Robotics and AI: CFD of fruit flies and free-flight robot tests show that the dorsal-ventral wing-beat asymmetry called wing-stroke dihedral passively steers a flapping flyer into a sideways gust (yaw); helps explain why the majority of flying insects have positive stroke dihedral (roll torques stabilise only at high gust speeds)

items.notes: Technology and engineering (bio-inspired flight) crossed with biology. Three links: most insects have the asymmetry; the asymmetry alone turns a flier into a gust; passive means through the ordinary wingbeat, not by changing it; conclusion: most insects can turn into gusts with no wing adjustment. Roll left out of the passage on purpose (the paper finds roll torques stabilise only at high gust speeds), so C is unsupported rather than contradicted.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Frontiers abstract (PMC8907628): stroke dihedral passively steers fliers into side gusts; most insects have positive stroke dihedral.

band7.why: Key joins three statements (most insects have the asymmetry, it acts by itself, passive means through the ordinary wingbeat); A keeps the right outcome with the active route, C a wrong motion; B, an invented comparison, is the easiest. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: The Haitian Revolution of 1791–1804, in which enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue overthrew both slavery and colonial rule, is often described as one of the most radical revolutions of the modern world. Yet in Freedom’s Mirror (2014), historian Ada Ferrer traces how those same events helped entrench slavery in Cuba, a Spanish colony barely fifty miles away. As Saint-Domingue’s plantations collapsed, Cuban planters rushed to fill the resulting gap in the international sugar market, while they and colonial authorities, determined to prevent “another Haiti,” worked to reinforce slavery on the island.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Although the Haitian Revolution brought an end to slavery in Saint-Domingue, Ferrer shows that it also helped make slavery more firmly established in neighboring Cuba.
Although historians often call the Haitian Revolution radical, Ferrer argues that its achievements were more limited than that label suggests, since slavery persisted nearby in Cuba.
Although Cuban planters profited from the collapse of Saint-Domingue’s plantations, Ferrer shows that the Haitian Revolution ultimately weakened slavery in Cuba by inspiring enslaved people there.
Although Cuban officials feared that a revolution like Haiti’s would spread to their island, Ferrer argues that those fears mainly reflected their wish to control Cuba’s sugar trade.
items.explanation: The text first notes that in Saint-Domingue enslaved people “overthrew both slavery and colonial rule.” It then turns (“Yet”) to Ferrer’s finding that the same events “helped entrench slavery in Cuba,” as planters filled “the resulting gap in the international sugar market” and authorities “worked to reinforce slavery on the island.” Choice A joins both halves: slavery ended in one place and grew stronger in the other.

B.why_wrong: Ferrer is not said to question how radical the revolution was; she traces its effects in Cuba, where slavery did not merely persist but was reinforced.

C.recipe: half-true compound (true first clause, contradicted finding)
C.why_wrong: Planters did profit from the collapse, but the text says the revolution “helped entrench slavery in Cuba,” not that it weakened slavery there.

D.recipe: half-true compound (true first clause, invented motive)
D.why_wrong: Officials did fear “another Haiti,” but the text gives no sign that Ferrer treats this fear as a cover for controlling the sugar trade; the two appear as parallel responses.

sources.what: Cambridge University Press book page for Ada Ferrer, Freedom's Mirror: Cuba and Haiti in the Age of Revolution (2014): the Haitian Revolution of 1791-1804, arguably the most radical revolution of the modern world; in Cuba, barely fifty miles away, it helped usher in the antithesis of revolutionary emancipation, as planters and authorities rushed to fill the void in the world sugar market, buttress slavery and colonial rule, and prevent another Haiti

items.notes: History (Atlantic world). View then correction: the revolution as a radical overthrow of slavery, then Ferrer's account of its opposite effect next door. Every option uses the Although frame (band-7 habit); B and D keep a true first clause and fail on the second; the key carries both halves. Fame check: the Haitian Revolution itself is known, but the Cuba argument and Ferrer's book are not textbook content, so background knowledge does not supply the key.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Cambridge UP description of Freedom's Mirror (2014): the revolution helped buttress slavery in Cuba, barely fifty miles away, as planters filled the sugar gap. Fame call: kept. The Haitian Revolution is classroom content, but the tested idea (it entrenched slavery in Cuba) is not, and background knowledge points to C, a wrong option.

band7.why: View then correction with a two-part key; B is the near miss that reads Ferrer as debunking the radical label, C the background-knowledge trap (the revolution inspiring Cuban slaves), D an invented motive. Key stays close to 'entrench' but must carry both halves. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Critics have long interpreted the furniture, fabrics, and other everyday objects in Victorian novels primarily for what those objects reveal about the characters who possess them. In The Ideas in Things (2006), literary scholar Elaine Freedgood contends that such objects can also be understood literally, as evidence of the actual histories through which they were manufactured and traded. The checked cotton curtains in the Barton family’s home in Elizabeth Gaskell’s 1848 novel Mary Barton, for example, lead Freedgood to the unpredictable international cotton market on which the novel’s Manchester households depended.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Freedgood argues that critics are wrong to read objects in Victorian novels as clues to character, since novelists such as Gaskell mainly meant them to record economic history.
Freedgood shows that the curtains in Mary Barton reveal how the Barton family’s fortunes rose and fell with changes in the global market for cotton.
Freedgood argues that objects in Victorian novels can point not only to traits of the characters who own them but also to the real-world production and commerce behind such goods.
Freedgood argues that Victorian readers, unlike modern critics, would have quickly seen the links between the objects in novels and the trade in those goods.
items.explanation: The text says that critics have interpreted everyday objects in Victorian novels “primarily for what those objects reveal about the characters who possess them,” and that Freedgood contends such objects “can also be understood literally, as evidence of the actual histories through which they were manufactured and traded.” The curtains in Mary Barton are her example. Choice C states the claim with both of its parts: objects still say something about characters, and they also lead to the making and selling of real goods.

A.recipe: too strong (replaces where the text adds) with an invented motive
A.why_wrong: Freedgood says objects “can also be understood literally”: she adds a way of reading them rather than calling the usual reading wrong, and the text says nothing about what novelists such as Gaskell meant the objects to do.

B.recipe: too narrow (the example taken for the main idea)
B.why_wrong: The curtains are only an example of Freedgood’s approach, and the text does not say they show the Bartons’ fortunes rising and falling; the main idea is the way of reading objects that the example illustrates.

D.why_wrong: The text never discusses what Victorian readers noticed; it contrasts the way critics have usually read such objects with the literal reading that Freedgood proposes.

sources.what: Review of Elaine Freedgood, The Ideas in Things: Fugitive Meaning in the Victorian Novel (University of Chicago Press, 2006), Romanticism and Victorianism on the Net 51 (2008): objects in Victorian fiction usually read chiefly for their capacity to illustrate character; Freedgood restores their lost meanings by reading them literally (strong metonymy), stressing how they were produced and circulated; examples include mahogany in Jane Eyre and cotton curtains in Mary Barton (chapter: Checked Curtains and Global Cotton Markets in Mary Barton). The blue-and-white check curtains in the Barton house checked in Gutenberg #2153, chapter 2.

items.notes: Arts and humanities (literary criticism), a scholar-argument main idea modelled on 3.20. Written in review to replace the L. A. Paul transformative-choice item, a concept clone of the live CID T1 hard w4b3_05 (Callard's Aspiration answers Paul). Two-part key: the usual character reading kept, Freedgood's literal reading added, paraphrased away from 'understood literally ... manufactured and traded'. A turns 'also' into 'instead' and adds an authorial motive, B takes the example for the main idea, D invents a comparison of readers. Fame: Mary Barton is not a classroom staple and Freedgood's method is not textbook content.

fixes: subject replaced: the L. A. Paul transformative-choice item was a concept clone of live central_ideas_and_details.T1.hard.w4b3_05 (Callard's Aspiration: decision theory fails for value-changing choices; same skill, template and tier, and Callard writes in reply to Paul); new item on Elaine Freedgood's The Ideas in Things, claimed in claims.txt, Paul claim withdrawn
the new item was written by the reviewer, so it has no independent blind solve
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: erudit.org review of The Ideas in Things (2006): objects usually read to illustrate character; Freedgood reads them literally for their production and circulation; cotton curtains in Mary Barton (Gaskell text checked for the Bartons' check curtains).

band7.why: Key keeps both halves (character reading kept, literal reading added); A is the 'instead of also' near miss with an invented motive, B the example taken for the thesis, D an invented comparison. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Computed tomography scans of an unnamed adult mummy from Egypt’s late New Kingdom, now held in the University of Sydney’s Chau Chak Wing Museum, revealed a mortuary treatment not previously documented: concealed beneath outer layers of linen, the body is encased in a mud shell coated with white pigment and painted red. Karin Sowada and colleagues concluded that the shell was a form of ancient conservation, applied to restore the body after it sustained damage. Royal mummies from the same period possess resin shells within their wrappings, and such resins were imported from the eastern Mediterranean at considerable expense.
items.stem: Which statement about the people who restored the body of the Chau Chak Wing Museum mummy is best supported by information in the text?
options: They likely restored royal mummies as well, since shells placed within the wrappings are also found on royal bodies of the period.
They likely intended the shell to be seen by mourners, since they took the trouble to coat it in white pigment and paint it red.
They likely chose mud over resin because mud was more effective than resin at holding a damaged body together.
They likely gave the body a treatment resembling that of royalty while using a material that was easier to obtain.
items.explanation: Royal mummies of the period “possess resin shells within their wrappings,” and this body has a similar shell “concealed beneath outer layers of linen.” But its shell is made of mud, whereas royal resins “were imported from the eastern Mediterranean at considerable expense.” Together these details suggest that the people who restored the body copied a royal treatment with a material that was easier to come by.

A.why_wrong: Royal mummies do have shells within their wrappings, but royal shells were resin, and nothing in the text links the people who used mud here to work on royal bodies.

B.why_wrong: The shell was painted, but it lies “beneath outer layers of linen,” so it was hidden from view rather than made for mourners to see.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how well mud and resin hold a body together; the difference it gives between them is that resin was a costly import.

sources.what: Sowada et al. 2021, PLoS ONE: CT scans of an unnamed late New Kingdom mummified adult in the Chau Chak Wing Museum, University of Sydney, show a mud carapace placed between linen layers, not previously documented; layers of mud, white calcite-based pigment and red paint; ancient conservation after post-mortem damage; interpreted as elite emulation of resin shells within royal wrappings; full text: resins imported from the eastern Mediterranean were expensive, and cheaper local alternatives allowed emulation of elite practice

items.notes: Archaeology (Egypt). Chain: royal mummies have resin shells inside the wrappings; this body has a mud shell in the same place; resin was a costly import; conclusion: the restorers imitated a royal treatment with a material easier to obtain (the authors' elite-emulation reading, which the passage leaves unstated). Hedged with likely, as the paper offers it as an interpretation.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PLoS ONE abstract and full text (PMC7857556): mud carapace between linen layers, not externally visible; elite emulation of royal resin shells; imported resins expensive.

band7.why: Key needs three premises (royal resin shells, same place in the wrappings, resin a costly import); A and C keep a true detail and fail on a later link; B falls to the stated concealment and is the easiest. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is from Ada Leverson’s 1908 novel Love’s Shadow. Edith and Bruce are a married couple.

‘Now I have to write that letter before I go,’ Bruce exclaimed, starting up and looking at her reproachfully. ‘Why didn’t I write it last night?’

Edith hadn’t the slightest idea, as she had heard nothing of the letter before, but, in the course of three years, she had learnt that it saved time to accept trifling injustices. So she looked guilty and a little remorseful. He magnanimously forgave her, and began to write the letter at a neat white writing-table.
items.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Bruce?
options: He faults Edith for a lapse that is his own, yet he regards himself as generous in how he treats her.
He is quick to forgive Edith, since he can see that she feels sorry about the delay with the letter.
He relies on Edith to keep track of his letters and is disappointed when she fails to remind him of one.
He is embarrassed about forgetting the letter and tries to finish it before Edith notices his oversight.
items.explanation: Bruce looks at Edith “reproachfully” over a letter he forgot, though she “had heard nothing of the letter before,” and the narrator calls his blame one of the “trifling injustices” she has learned to accept. When she only pretends to be “guilty and a little remorseful,” he “magnanimously forgave her”: the word is ironic, since there was nothing to forgive, but it shows that Bruce sees himself as generous.

B.recipe: literal misreading (takes the irony at face value)
B.why_wrong: Edith only “looked guilty” to save time; she had done nothing wrong, so Bruce’s forgiveness is not real kindness toward a sorry wife but part of his unfair blame.

C.why_wrong: Bruce does act as if Edith should have reminded him, but she “had heard nothing of the letter before,” so she could not have been keeping track of it for him.

D.why_wrong: Bruce announces the letter to Edith himself and blames her for it; nothing suggests he is embarrassed or hiding the oversight.

sources.what: Ada Leverson, Love's Shadow (first published London, 1908), Project Gutenberg #9786, chapter I; excerpt copied exactly (single quotes set curly)

items.notes: Literary prose irony (T6 literary variant, band-7 recipe section 5): the narrator's 'magnanimously' is ironic, since Edith has nothing to be forgiven for. Key frame '[does A], yet [B]'. Distractors: the surface reading (B), a half-true reliance claim (C), a contradiction (D). Excerpt copied from Gutenberg #9786 with no changes beyond curly quotes; Raggett spelling exchange that follows was trimmed at a paragraph boundary to keep the length near the models.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg #9786, chapter I: exact.

band7.why: Irony item: the key needs both the unfair blame and the irony of 'magnanimously'; B takes the irony at face value, C is half true (he does act as if she should have reminded him). CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Louise Imogen Guiney’s 1898 poem “Doves.” Bow and Paul’s are churches in London.

Ah, if man’s boast and man’s advance be vain!
And yonder bells of Bow, loud-echoing home,
And the lone Tree, foreknow it, and the Dome,
That monstrous island of the middle main;
If each inheritor must sink again
Under his sires, as falleth where it [climbed]
Back on the gone wave the disheartened foam?—
I crossed Cheapside, and this was in my brain.
What folly lies in forecasts and in fears!
Like a wide laughter sweet and opportune,
Wet from the fount, three hundred doves of Paul’s
Shook their warm wings, drizzling the golden noon,
And in their rain-cloud vanished up the walls.
“God keeps,” I said, “our little flock of years.”
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker’s fear that London’s great buildings will someday fall seems to be confirmed when the doves suddenly abandon the walls of Paul’s.
The speaker, crossing Cheapside, worries that human progress is futile, since each generation seems to sink back to the level of the one before it.
The speaker’s gloomy thoughts about whether human achievement can last give way to reassurance when she sees a flock of doves take flight.
The speaker contrasts the doves’ freedom with the burden of human ambition and decides that people should give up striving for progress.
items.explanation: The first eight lines ask what would follow if “man’s boast and man’s advance be vain,” with each generation sinking back like foam on a wave; this “was in my brain” as the speaker crossed Cheapside. Then the doves of Paul’s rise “like a wide laughter,” she calls her fears “folly,” and she concludes that God “keeps” our “little flock of years.” Her gloom gives way to reassurance.

A.why_wrong: The doves “vanished up the walls” in a burst the speaker compares to laughter, and she then dismisses her “forecasts” and “fears”; nothing is confirmed.

B.why_wrong: This covers only the opening lines. Once the doves of Paul’s rise, the speaker calls such worry “folly” and concludes that “God keeps” our “little flock of years,” so the poem ends in reassurance, not worry.

D.why_wrong: The speaker does wonder whether human “advance” is “vain,” but the doves lead her to reject that worry as “folly,” not to conclude that people should stop striving.

sources.what: Louise Imogen Guiney, England and Yesterday: A Book of Short Poems (London: Grant Richards, 1898), London sonnets, VII Doves; Project Gutenberg #52533; copied exactly except clomb replaced by [climbed]

items.notes: Literary poem (sonnet). Extended figure: human generations as foam falling back on a wave, answered by the doves and the closing image of years as a flock God keeps. Key carries the turn (gloom, then reassurance). Gloss line covers Bow and Paul's (Cheapside is plainly a place the speaker crosses); 'clomb' bracketed as [climbed] in CB's adaptation style, so the source line says adapted. Length runs above the two models (a full sonnet plus a gloss line), within the official literary range.

fixes: gloss trimmed to Bow and Paul's (Cheapside is plainly a place she crosses): 139 to 131 words, at the longest hard poem model (3.17, 133); a sonnet cannot be cut
B rebuilt as the near miss that stops before the turn (was 'hardly notices the doves', killed by the climax)
review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg #52533 (England and Yesterday, 1898), VII Doves: exact except clomb glossed as [climbed].

band7.why: Hard sonnet with archaic syntax and a volta; B now the near miss that stops before the turn, D half true (real doubt, invented conclusion), A a literal misreading of the doves. CID hard cells are planned as band 6 (WAVE.md); a strong band 6.

items.passage: Conservation plans for the Florida manatee have generally assumed that the animals were historically at least as numerous and widespread as they are today. To evaluate that assumption, anthropologists Thomas Pluckhahn and David Thulman examined reports of manatee remains from archaeological excavations throughout Florida, along with documentary accounts of manatee sightings from the colonial era onward. Surprisingly, the evidence indicates that Florida’s manatee population remained very small until the nineteenth century, when the animals began expanding in number and range alongside the state’s growing human population.
items.stem: According to the text, what was surprising about the evidence that Pluckhahn and Thulman reviewed?
options: It confirmed that manatees were once as numerous and widespread in Florida as conservation plans had assumed.
It suggested that manatees were scarce in Florida for a long period and grew more common only in the nineteenth century.
It showed that hunting by Florida’s early peoples had greatly reduced the number of manatees in the region.
It revealed that manatees became more common in Florida as the state’s human population declined.
items.explanation: The text marks the surprise directly: “Surprisingly, the evidence indicates that Florida’s manatee population remained very small until the nineteenth century, when the animals began expanding in number and range alongside the state’s growing human population.” Choice B restates this: manatees were scarce in Florida for a long period and became more common only in the nineteenth century.

A.why_wrong: The evidence challenged the assumption that manatees were “historically at least as numerous and widespread as they are today”; it showed a population that “remained very small until the nineteenth century.”

C.why_wrong: The text never mentions hunting; it reports that the population was small before the nineteenth century but gives no cause for this.

D.why_wrong: Manatees expanded in number and range “alongside the state’s growing human population,” not as that population declined.

sources.what: Pluckhahn and Thulman 2024, PLoS ONE 19(11): e0313070, Historical ecology reveals the 'surprising' direction and extent of shifting baselines for the Florida manatee: systematic and opportunistic reviews of archaeological and historical records; populations very small in the Precolonial and Colonial Periods; expansion in number and range in the Territorial/Early Statehood (from 1821) and Early Modern Periods, tracking human population growth and landscape change; contrary to the assumption that manatees were as or more numerous and widespread in the past

items.notes: Natural science (historical ecology). Explicit detail with the 'what was surprising' frame (2.16): the text marks the surprise and the key restates it in other words. Written in review to replace the Arctic hare migration item, too close to the earlier-claimed Arctic fox Svalbard-to-Ellesmere item (words_in_context.B3.easy.w5b1_24). Simplified: the Territorial Period, from 1821, rendered as the nineteenth century; landscape and policy changes behind the expansion left out.

fixes: subject replaced: Arctic hares satellite-tracked at Alert, Ellesmere Island were too close to the earlier-claimed Arctic fox tracked from Svalbard to Ellesmere (words_in_context.B3.easy.w5b1_24, staged); new item on the Florida manatee historical baseline (Pluckhahn and Thulman 2024), claimed, hare claim withdrawn
the new item was written by the reviewer, so it has no independent blind solve
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PLoS ONE full text (PMC11578630): populations very small in the Precolonial and Colonial Periods, expanding from the nineteenth century with human population; contrary to the assumed baseline.

items.passage: Medieval scribes wrote on parchment made from animal skins, and thirteenth-century records from Beaulieu Abbey in England show that calfskin was scarcer and more expensive than sheepskin. Analyzing collagen from nearly every surviving book and charter of Orval Abbey, a monastery in present-day Belgium, historian Nicolas Ruffini-Ronzani and colleagues found that the abbey’s own scribes used the two skins about equally for books, favoring calfskin for higher-quality volumes. The charters followed a different pattern: although the five earliest were written on calfskin, every charter from the 1230s onward was written on sheepskin.
items.stem: According to the text, what is a difference between the books made by Orval Abbey’s scribes and the abbey’s charters from the 1230s onward?
options: The books were made from both calfskin and sheepskin, whereas the charters were made only from sheepskin.
The books were made mostly from calfskin that the abbey bought from Beaulieu Abbey, whereas the charters were made from local sheepskin.
The books were made only from sheepskin, whereas the charters were made from calfskin because they were considered more important.
The books were made from parchment that cost less than the parchment used for the charters, since books were copied more often.
items.explanation: The text says that Orval’s scribes “used the two skins about equally for books,” while “every charter from the 1230s onward was written on sheepskin.” So the books used both calfskin and sheepskin, but the later charters used only sheepskin.

B.why_wrong: Beaulieu Abbey appears only as the source of records about parchment prices; the text never says Orval bought calfskin from it, and Orval’s books used the two skins about equally.

C.why_wrong: This reverses the pattern: the books used both skins, and the charters from the 1230s onward were all sheepskin.

D.why_wrong: The books often used calfskin, the costlier skin, while the later charters used only sheepskin, so the books’ parchment was not the cheaper of the two; the text also says nothing about how often books were copied.

sources.what: Ruffini-Ronzani et al. 2021, Royal Society Open Science: ZooMS species identification of parchment collagen from almost the entire library and all charters of Orval Abbey, Belgium; Orval scriptorium books balanced calfskin (47.1%) and sheepskin (48.5%), calfskin preferred for higher-quality manuscripts; consistent with 13th-century Beaulieu Abbey accounts where calfskin was scarcer and pricier; five earliest charters calfskin, all charters from the 1230s onward sheepskin

items.notes: History (medieval book history). Explicit detail with the 'what is a difference' frame (2.26): the key joins the books sentence and the charters sentence. Simplified: 'nearly every surviving book' for almost the entire library and all single-leaf charters; ZooMS described as analyzing collagen.

fixes: 'reserving calfskin' softened to 'favoring calfskin' (the source says calfskin was preferably used for higher-quality manuscripts)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: R. Soc. Open Sci. abstract (PMC8170200).

items.passage: As once-isolated communities become more connected to the wider world, traditional practices can be replaced by new ones. To examine this process, anthropologist Gul Deniz Salali and colleagues interviewed Mbendjele BaYaka, hunter-gatherers in the Republic of Congo, about the wild plants they know and use. Compared with BaYaka born in forest camps, BaYaka born in a logging town reported knowing and using fewer plants, and the uses they lacked were mostly medicinal. The town-born participants also said that they preferred Western medicine to traditional remedies.
items.stem: What does the text indicate about the BaYaka participants who were born in a logging town?
options: They knew of many plants that grow near towns but not in the forests where other BaYaka live.
They had learned most of what they knew about plants from Western doctors rather than from relatives.
They knew as many plants as forest-born BaYaka did but used those plants less often.
They knew less than forest-born BaYaka did about wild plants, particularly plants used as medicine.
items.explanation: The text says that, compared with forest-born BaYaka, those born in a logging town “reported knowing and using fewer plants, and the uses they lacked were mostly medicinal.” Choice D restates this: the town-born participants knew less about wild plants, especially medicinal ones.

A.why_wrong: The text never mentions plants that grow only near towns; it reports only that town-born BaYaka knew fewer plants.

B.recipe: twisted detail (preference turned into a source)
B.why_wrong: The town-born participants said they “preferred Western medicine,” but the text does not say they learned about plants from Western doctors.

C.why_wrong: They reported knowing fewer plants, not as many.

sources.what: Salali et al. 2020, Evolutionary Human Sciences (Global WEIRDing): Mbendjele BaYaka hunter-gatherers of the Republic of Congo; town-born BaYaka (a logging town) reported knowing and using fewer plants than forest-born BaYaka; the lost uses related to medicine; town-born preferred Western medicine over traditional practices

items.notes: Social science (anthropology). Explicit detail, 'What does the text indicate about X?' frame (2.3, 2.14). Key paraphrases 'fewer plants' and 'mostly medicinal'. The study's age difference between groups (all town-born participants under 45) is left out; no option depends on it.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Evol. Hum. Sci. abstract (PMC10427474).

items.passage: Red paints in ancient rock art were generally manufactured from iron-rich mineral deposits. But when archaeological scientist Brandi Lee MacDonald and colleagues analyzed paint from a pictograph panel at Boling Point, on Babine Lake in British Columbia, they found that its iron oxide had been produced by Leptothrix ochracea, a bacterium that forms iron-rich mats in water. The pigment’s magnetic and structural properties showed that local hunter-gatherers had harvested these mats and heated them in hearths to between 750°C and 850°C, making the paint’s color stronger and more durable.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers have determined that most rock art in British Columbia was painted with pigment made from bacteria rather than from minerals.
Researchers found that hunter-gatherers made the paint for a pictograph by collecting and heating a substance produced by bacteria.
The bacterium Leptothrix ochracea forms red mats when sunlight heats the shallow water in which the bacterium lives.
Hunter-gatherers at Babine Lake used bacterial mats for paint because there were no iron-rich mineral deposits in the region.
items.explanation: The text reports that the iron oxide in the Boling Point paint “had been produced by Leptothrix ochracea, a bacterium,” and that hunter-gatherers “had harvested these mats and heated them in hearths.” Choice B states this finding, with the bacterial mats abstracted as a substance produced by bacteria.

A.why_wrong: The researchers analyzed paint from one pictograph panel; the text does not say that most rock art in the province used bacterial pigment.

C.why_wrong: The heating described in the text was done by people “in hearths,” not by sunlight in shallow water.

D.why_wrong: The text never says why the hunter-gatherers chose bacterial mats or that mineral deposits were missing near Babine Lake.

sources.what: MacDonald et al. 2019, Scientific Reports: rock art paint from the Boling Point pictograph panel (GcSi-1), Babine Lake, British Columbia, made from iron oxide produced by the bacterium Leptothrix ochracea; hunter-gatherers harvested aquatic microbial iron mats and heated them in open hearths at 750-850 C to enhance color and colorfastness

items.notes: Archaeology (Pacific Northwest rock art). Study report: usual source, then the finding and method. Key abstracts the bacterial mats as 'a substance produced by bacteria' (house abstraction, 2.12). Distractors: too broad (A), twisted mechanism (C), unsupported motive (D).

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Sci. Rep. abstract (PMC6864057).

items.passage: Ravens are significant nest predators of ground-nesting birds such as the black grouse. Richard Policht and colleagues discovered, however, that adult black grouse also became attentive to raven calls outside the breeding season, when the birds had no nests to protect. In playback experiments, the grouse recognized raven calls, stretching their necks, scanning their surroundings, and eventually fleeing. Since ravens do not directly threaten adult grouse, the researchers propose that the response may be acquired early in life from nesting hens or that raven calls may signal the proximity of red foxes.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that black grouse hens react more strongly to raven calls than other adults do because hens must guard their nests.
Ravens have become a growing threat to adult black grouse outside the breeding season, when the grouse are less watchful.
Adult black grouse recognize and react to the calls of ravens even though ravens pose no direct danger to them, a finding that researchers have tried to explain.
Black grouse learn to avoid red foxes by listening for the calls of the ravens that hunt alongside the foxes.
items.explanation: The text reports that adult black grouse “recognized raven calls” and reacted to them “outside the breeding season,” although “ravens do not directly threaten adult grouse.” It ends with the researchers’ possible explanations. Choice C joins the finding to the puzzle that the researchers try to explain.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares hens with other adults; it describes adult grouse reacting when they “had no nests to protect.”

B.why_wrong: The text says that ravens “do not directly threaten adult grouse,” so they are not described as a growing danger to the adults.

D.why_wrong: The researchers only “propose” that raven calls “may signal the proximity of red foxes”; the text does not say ravens hunt alongside foxes or that grouse have learned this.

sources.what: Policht et al. 2019, PeerJ: adult black grouse alerted by raven calls outside the breeding season; playbacks showed recognition (neck stretching, head scanning, escape); ravens do not directly endanger adults; proposed explanations: a response learned as juveniles from nesting hens, or ravens' association with red foxes

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Main idea spread across the passage (finding plus unexplained puzzle), as in the medium spread-type items. Left out: males reacted faster than females (so A is unsupported, not contradicted).

fixes: 'occasionally fleeing' changed to 'eventually fleeing' (the abstract: neck stretching, head scanning and eventual escape)
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PeerJ abstract (PMC6422015).

items.passage: Netherlandish painters of the seventeenth century who worked on wooden panels most frequently chose oak. When Marta Domínguez-Delmás and colleagues used X-ray computed tomography to examine a panel painting attributed to the Antwerp studio of Peter Paul Rubens, they discovered that it consists of two boards glued together, a construction concealed by oak strips covering all four edges. The back board, the only one externally visible, is oak. The front board, on which the image was originally painted, is a tropical wood, probably mahogany, that was rarely employed in Netherlandish paintings.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about the painting?
options: Someone examining only its back and edges would likely assume that it had been painted on an ordinary oak panel.
It was likely painted far from Antwerp, in a region where the tropical wood of its front board grew.
It was likely painted earlier than most works from Rubens’s studio, since oak panels became less common over time.
Its image was likely painted on the oak board first and later transferred to the tropical board to protect it.
items.explanation: The back board, “the only one externally visible,” is oak, and the boundary between the two boards is hidden by “oak strips covering all four edges.” Since oak was the usual wood for such panels, anyone seeing only the back and edges would likely assume the painting was on an ordinary oak panel, even though the image is on “a tropical wood.”

B.why_wrong: The painting is attributed to Rubens’s studio in Antwerp; a front board of tropical wood shows only that the studio used an unusual imported wood, not that the work was painted where that wood grew.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about when oak panels became less common or how this painting’s date compares with other works from the studio.

D.why_wrong: The text says the image was painted on the front, tropical board, so it was not first painted on the oak board.

sources.what: Dominguez-Delmas et al. 2021, PLoS ONE: X-ray CT of a panel painting attributed to Rubens' studio revealed a double panelling concealed by oak strips on all four edges; back (visible) board deciduous oak, the most common wood in 17th-century Netherlandish workshops; front (original) board a tropical wood, probably Swietenia (mahogany), seldom used in Netherlandish paintings; oak board possibly glued on to pretend the painting was on oak

items.notes: Arts and humanities (technical art history). P1: oak was the usual wood for panels; P2: only the oak back board is visible and the edges are covered with oak strips; conclusion: the panel would pass for oak (the authors raise deceptive intent as one possibility; the key stays with what a viewer would assume). Antwerp added from general knowledge of Rubens's studio.

fixes: B rewritten: 'painted somewhere outside the Netherlands' read as true to a student who knows Antwerp is in Belgium; now 'far from Antwerp, where the tropical wood grew'
review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PLoS ONE abstract (PMC8396786).

items.passage: Leopards are not currently found in Taiwan, and no historical documents mention their presence on the island. In Longshia-dong Cave, in southern Taiwan’s Kenting National Park, however, Tzu-Chin Chi and colleagues investigated three fossilized teeth, all from the same individual, that date to the Late Pleistocene epoch. The teeth closely resemble those of modern leopards in both dimensions and morphology, and they differ from those of the clouded leopards and tigers that also inhabit Asia. The teeth are somewhat smaller than those of fossil leopards discovered in China.
items.stem: Based on the text, what can most reasonably be concluded about leopards in Taiwan?
options: They were likely larger than the leopards that lived in what is now China during the Late Pleistocene.
They were likely more closely related to clouded leopards than to the leopards found elsewhere in Asia.
They likely lived only in the area around Kenting, since no leopard fossils have been found elsewhere on the island.
They likely disappeared from the island before people began keeping written records of its animals.
items.explanation: The fossil teeth show that leopards lived in Taiwan during the Late Pleistocene, yet leopards “are not currently found in Taiwan,” and “no historical documents mention their presence on the island.” Together these facts suggest that leopards died out in Taiwan before people began recording the island’s animals.

A.why_wrong: The teeth are “somewhat smaller than those of fossil leopards discovered in China,” not larger.

B.why_wrong: The teeth “closely resemble those of modern leopards” and “differ from those of the clouded leopards,” so the text gives no reason to link them to clouded leopards.

C.recipe: overstated (absence of evidence taken as evidence)
C.why_wrong: The text describes fossils from one cave; it never says that other parts of Taiwan have been searched or that leopards lived only near Kenting.

sources.what: Chi, Gan, Yang and Chang 2021, PeerJ: three fossil leopard (Panthera pardus) teeth from one individual in Longshia-dong Cave, Kenting National Park, southern Taiwan; no historical literature mentions leopards in Taiwan and they are not present there; teeth match extant leopards in size and shape, compared with clouded leopards and tigers; first report of leopards in Late Pleistocene Taiwan; smaller than Chinese fossil leopards

items.notes: Natural science (paleontology), modelled on 2.19's two-premise inference. P1: no leopards now and none in historical records; P2: Late Pleistocene leopard teeth; conclusion: they disappeared before written records. 'Large cat' generalises the paper's pantherine assignment.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PeerJ abstract (PMC8388558).

items.passage: T’boli weaver Lang Dulay (1928–2015), of Lake Sebu in the southern Philippines, devoted her life to producing t’nalak, a cloth woven from dyed abaca fiber. As the craft became increasingly commercialized and outsiders introduced more modern designs, Dulay remained faithful to traditional T’boli motifs, retaining a repertoire of about 100 patterns in her memory, some of them based on her dreams. She also established a workshop in her hometown to promote the traditional art, and by 2014 five of her grandchildren had become weavers.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Dulay became known for creating modern designs that helped t’nalak appeal to buyers outside Lake Sebu.
Dulay learned the traditional patterns of t’nalak at a workshop that T’boli elders had set up in her hometown.
Dulay worked to keep a traditional form of T’boli weaving alive and to pass it on to younger weavers.
Dulay’s t’nalak cloth is widely admired for its bright colors, which come from dyes she invented herself.
items.explanation: While others “introduced more modern designs,” Dulay “remained faithful to traditional T’boli motifs,” and she “established a workshop in her hometown to promote the traditional art,” after which “five of her grandchildren had become weavers.” Choice C sums up both efforts: preserving the tradition and passing it on.

A.why_wrong: It was outsiders who “introduced more modern designs”; Dulay remained faithful to traditional motifs.

B.recipe: twisted detail (who set up the workshop)
B.why_wrong: Dulay herself established the workshop to promote the art; the text does not say she learned weaving at a workshop run by elders.

D.why_wrong: The text mentions that the abaca fiber is dyed, but it says nothing about bright colors, praise for them, or dyes Dulay invented.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Lang Dulay: T'boli weaver from Lake Sebu, South Cotabato (1928-2015), National Living Treasures Award 1998; preserved T'nalak weaving (dyed abaca fibre); kept traditional motifs amid commercialization and modern designs by non-T'bolis; repertoire of about 100 patterns, some based on dreams; set up the Manlilikha ng Bayan Center workshop in her hometown; by 2014 five grandchildren were weavers

items.notes: Arts and humanities (textile art). Profile: person and aim, two concrete efforts, effect. Key generalises the examples into preserving and passing on the tradition (2.6 style). Distractor recipes from the T3 blueprint: contradiction, twisted example, invented reputation.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Wikipedia, Lang Dulay.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sigrid Undset’s 1911 novel Jenny (translated by W. Emmé in 1921). Helge Gram, a Norwegian traveler, is observing a crowded thoroughfare in Rome.

He stood still, watching the stream run past him, and smiled at the thought that he could drift along this street every evening in the dusk among the crowds, until it became as familiar to him as the best-known thoroughfare of his own city—Christiania. He was suddenly seized with the wish to walk and walk—now and all night maybe—through all the streets of Rome.

Everything else he had seen on his journey had disappointed him, for it was not what he had imagined at home when he had been longing to go abroad and see it all. One sight at last was far beyond his dreams, and that was Rome.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Helge misses his own city and hopes that Rome will someday feel as familiar to him as Christiania does.
After a journey that has mostly let him down, Helge is delighted to find a city that exceeds what he had imagined.
Helge is overwhelmed by the crowds of Rome and wishes that he could return to the quiet streets of home.
Helge regrets that he imagined Rome so vividly before his trip, because the city has failed to match his expectations.
items.explanation: The narrator says that “everything else he had seen on his journey had disappointed him,” but “one sight at last was far beyond his dreams, and that was Rome.” His smile and his sudden “wish to walk and walk” through the city show his delight. Choice B joins the disappointment of the journey with his joy in Rome.

A.why_wrong: Helge does imagine this street becoming as familiar as one in Christiania, but he smiles at the thought as a pleasure of living in Rome, not out of homesickness.

C.why_wrong: Helge enjoys drifting “among the crowds” and wants to walk all night through Rome; nothing suggests he is overwhelmed or wants to go home.

D.why_wrong: It was the other sights of the journey that disappointed him; Rome was “far beyond his dreams.”

sources.what: Sigrid Undset, Jenny: A Novel, translated from the Norwegian by W. Emmé (New York: Knopf, 1921), Part One, chapter I; Project Gutenberg #60741; trimmed at sentence boundaries (the Pincio paragraph and the clause after 'streets of Rome' left out), so the source line says adapted; Norwegian original published 1911

items.notes: Literary prose (translation, Norwegian). Key carries the contrast (disappointing journey, delight in Rome) in CB's literary key frame. Distractors: half-true homesickness (A), opposite feeling (C), twisted object of disappointment (D).

fixes: context line shortened: 152 to 139 words, near the models' median 141; A's why_wrong no longer names the Corso
review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg #60741 (Emmé translation, 1921), chapter I: exact apart from the noted trims.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: The speaker considers how grand or menacing ordinary objects must seem from the point of view of a very small creature.
The speaker warns that small things such as thorns and wasps can be as dangerous to people as spears and leopards.
The speaker describes a fly’s search for food as it moves from a rosebud to a loaf of bread and some salt.
The speaker admires the fly for facing dangers that would frighten much larger animals, such as leopards and lambs.
items.explanation: The poem opens, “How large unto the tiny fly / Must little things appear!” and then lists everyday objects as a fly might see them: a rosebud becomes “a feather bed,” a loaf of bread “a lofty hill,” and a wasp “a cruel leopard.” Choice A states this idea: small, ordinary things would seem huge or threatening to so small a creature.

B.why_wrong: The comparisons describe how things appear to the fly; the poem does not warn that thorns or wasps are as dangerous to people as spears or leopards.

C.why_wrong: The poem lists separate images of how things would look to a fly; it does not tell of a fly moving from one object to another in search of food.

D.why_wrong: Leopards and lambs appear only in comparisons; the speaker never praises the fly’s courage or compares it with other animals.

sources.what: Walter de la Mare (as Walter Ramal), Songs of Childhood (London: Longmans, Green, 1902), The Fly; Project Gutenberg #23545; copied exactly, double hyphen set as a closed em dash, indentation dropped

items.notes: Literary poem. One extended figure (everyday things at a fly's scale) carried into a general statement, as in medium poem main-idea items. The poet is well known but this children's poem is not a classroom staple; the main idea comes from the opening lines, not background knowledge.

review.facts_note: Excerpt checked against Gutenberg #23545 (Songs of Childhood, 1902): exact.

items.passage: The Imdang cemetery in Gyeongsan, South Korea, contains the graves of people from Apdok, an early state on the Korean Peninsula. To reconstruct the diet of these people, archaeologist Kyungcheol Choy and his team measured chemical signatures called stable isotopes in human and animal skeletons from the graves. The results indicated that game birds were the largest component of the Imdang diet, followed by plants. The team also discovered that elites consumed more game birds and seafood than the attendants buried with them.
items.stem: According to the text, what did the researchers find about the diet of the people buried at Imdang?
options: It came mostly from animals raised on farms near the cemetery.
It included very few plants of any kind.
It was the same for elites and for their attendants.
Game birds made up more of it than any other food did.
items.explanation: The text states that “game birds were the largest component of the Imdang diet, followed by plants.” Choice D restates this finding.

A.why_wrong: The text says the largest part of the diet was game birds, which are hunted, and it never mentions farm animals raised near the cemetery.

B.why_wrong: Plants were the second largest part of the diet, so the people did not eat very few plants.

C.why_wrong: The team found that “elites consumed more game birds and seafood than the attendants buried with them.”

sources.what: Choy et al. 2021, Scientific Reports: stable isotope ratios from humans and animals at the Imdang cemetery, Gyeongsan, South Korea (early Apdok state); dietary sources game birds > C3 plants > terrestrial herbivores > marine fish > C4 plants; elites consumed more game birds than their retainers and also seafood

items.notes: Archaeology (Korea). Explicit detail, easy: the key restates one sentence. 'Retainers' rendered as attendants; C3 plants simplified to plants.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Sci. Rep. abstract (PMC8605008).

items.passage: Many schools and libraries in rural Malawi have no internet connection, so students there cannot easily research information. Through a program called World Librarians, Charles Schweik and his colleagues set up solar-powered computer labs in some of these schools and libraries. Teachers and librarians then submit requests for the materials their communities want, rather than receiving what outsiders consider necessary. Searchers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst find the information and send it back as digital files.
items.stem: According to the text, how does World Librarians decide what information to provide to schools and libraries?
options: It provides the books that are most often borrowed from libraries in the United States.
It lets students search the internet for themselves in the new computer labs.
It provides the materials that teachers and librarians ask for.
It provides only information about science and technology.
items.explanation: The text says that “teachers and librarians then submit requests for the materials their communities want,” which searchers in Massachusetts then find and send back. Choice C restates this.

A.why_wrong: The program sends what communities request “rather than” what outsiders think they need; it does not choose popular American books.

B.why_wrong: The schools have “no internet connection,” which is why searchers elsewhere find the information for them.

D.why_wrong: The text never limits the requests to science and technology.

sources.what: Schweik, Meyer, Chinkondenji, Smith and Mchenga 2020, World Development Perspectives: World Librarians sets up solar-powered computer labs in remote offline schools and libraries in Malawi and provides the digital information they want rather than what the Global North thinks they need; requests from Requester nodes are handled by a Searcher node at the University of Massachusetts Amherst; large files sent via teacher or librarian cell phones

items.notes: Social science (education and development). Explicit detail, easy, 'how did/does' method frame (2.23). Key echoes the request sentence, as easy keys do.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: World Dev. Perspect. abstract (PMC7468314).

items.passage: Most modern iguanas excavate burrows for shelter or for laying eggs, but until recently no such burrow had been identified in the fossil record. In 2020, paleontologist Anthony Martin and his colleagues described a burrow approximately 115,000 years old preserved in sedimentary rock on San Salvador Island in the Bahamas. The burrow matches the dimensions and shape of the nesting burrows that modern iguanas dig. It was also filled in from the inside, just as modern iguanas fill their nests after depositing eggs.
items.stem: According to the text, why do the researchers think the fossil burrow was made by an iguana?
options: The bones of an iguana were found inside the burrow.
The burrow resembles the nesting burrows that modern iguanas make.
The burrow contains marks left by an iguana’s claws.
The burrow is the oldest one ever found in the Bahamas.
items.explanation: The text explains that the burrow “matches the dimensions and shape of the nesting burrows that modern iguanas dig” and was filled in “just as modern iguanas fill their nests.” Choice B states this reason.

A.why_wrong: The text never mentions bones; the identification rests on the burrow’s size, shape, and filling.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about claw marks.

D.why_wrong: The text calls the burrow the first fossil iguana burrow identified, not the oldest burrow of any kind in the Bahamas, and age is not the reason given for linking it to iguanas.

sources.what: Martin et al. 2020, PLoS ONE: first known fossil iguana nesting burrow, Grotto Beach Formation (about 115 ka), San Salvador Island, The Bahamas; matches dimensions and forms of modern iguana burrows; internal structures show active backfilling consistent with modern iguana nesting burrows; most modern iguanas dig burrows for dwelling and nesting

items.notes: Natural science (paleontology, trace fossils). Explicit detail with a reason frame (1.19). 'Active backfilling' rendered as filled in from the inside.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: PLoS ONE abstract (PMC7725343).

items.passage: Foraging at dawn is costly for pollinators such as bumblebees, whose eyes are adapted to daytime vision. Katie Hall, Natalie Hempel de Ibarra, and their team attached RFID tags to bumblebee foragers to record when each bee departed from the colony in the morning. Most foragers waited until light levels were high. However, the bees that departed earliest, in dim light, tended to be larger. Larger bumblebees have more sensitive eyes, which may help them locate flowers when light is limited.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that the bumblebees that start visiting flowers in dim morning light tend to be bigger than other bumblebees.
Researchers found that bumblebees prefer to visit flowers at dawn because flowers hold the most nectar early in the day.
Smaller bumblebees have more sensitive eyes than larger bumblebees do.
Most bumblebees leave their colony before sunrise to avoid the predators that hunt during the day.
items.explanation: The text reports that “most foragers waited until light levels were high,” but “the bees that departed earliest, in dim light, tended to be larger.” Choice A states this finding.

B.why_wrong: The text never discusses nectar, and it says most foragers waited for bright light rather than preferring dawn.

C.why_wrong: The text says that larger bumblebees have more sensitive eyes.

D.why_wrong: Most foragers waited until light levels were high, and the text says nothing about predators.

sources.what: Hall, Robert, Gaston and Hempel de Ibarra 2021, Ecology and Evolution: RFID tracking of Bombus terrestris foragers; bees leaving the colony earlier and at lower light levels were larger; larger foragers aided by more sensitive eyes; most foragers left at higher light levels; low light is an extra cost for pollinators with diurnal vision

items.notes: Natural science (animal behavior). Study report in four short moves (problem, method, finding, explanation), easy register. The paper's finding that foraging experience also mattered is left out.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: Ecol. Evol. abstract (PMC8207423).

items.passage: Borana Oromo pastoralists in southern Ethiopia still rely on indigenous knowledge in decisions about their herds and livelihoods. In a study conducted in 2021, Abera Bekele Dinsa and his colleagues worked with knowledgeable community members to learn how they forecast the coming rainy and dry seasons. The researchers found that the pastoralists watch the Moon closely, noting the tilt of the new Moon, any ring that forms around it, and its color. These indicators give warning well before a season begins.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Researchers found that Borana Oromo forecasts are more accurate than those made by Ethiopia’s national weather service.
Borana Oromo pastoralists have stopped using traditional forecasts because of the severe droughts of recent years.
Researchers found that Borana Oromo pastoralists predict seasonal weather by observing features of the Moon.
Borana Oromo elders track the movements of the stars to decide when to lead their herds to new pastures.
items.explanation: The study set out to learn how the pastoralists “forecast the coming rainy and dry seasons,” and it found that they “watch the Moon closely,” noting its tilt, rings, and color. Choice C states this finding.

A.why_wrong: The text never compares Borana forecasts with those of a national weather service.

B.why_wrong: The text says the pastoralists “still rely on indigenous knowledge.”

D.recipe: twisted detail (stars instead of the Moon)
D.why_wrong: The signs described are features of the Moon, not the movements of stars, and the text does not say they are used to choose pastures.

sources.what: Dinsa, Wakjira, Demmesie and Negash 2022, F1000Research: Borana Oromo pastoralists of southern Ethiopia forecast seasonal weather from features of the Moon (inclination of the first-date new moon, ring or cloud around the moon, colour); data from focus groups and knowledgeable groups in 2021; gives lead time before a season; still used in livelihood decisions

items.notes: Social science (traditional ecological knowledge). Study report, easy register; the governing claim sits in the third sentence. The paper's relative-accuracy claim is left out so option A stays plainly unsupported.

review.facts_note: Core claim confirmed: F1000Research abstract (PMC10726095).

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Hugh Walpole’s 1923 novel Jeremy and Hamlet. Hamlet is a dog belonging to a boy named Jeremy Cole, whose family’s kitchen is located in the basement of their house.

He was an older dog than he had been on that snowy occasion of his first meeting with the Cole family—two years older in fact. Older and fatter. He had now a round belly.

He had sold his soul to the cook.

Had Jeremy, his master, not gone to school, Hamlet’s soul would yet have been his own; Jeremy gone, Hamlet’s spiritual life was nobody’s concern. He fell down, deep down, into the very heart of the basement, and nobody minded.

He himself did not mind; he was very glad. He loved the basement.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Hamlet is lonely and unhappy now that Jeremy has gone away to school.
Hamlet has been shut in the basement as a punishment for growing too fat.
Hamlet waits eagerly in the basement for Jeremy to come home from school.
With Jeremy away at school, Hamlet has happily attached himself to the cook and the kitchen.
items.explanation: With Jeremy “gone” to school, Hamlet “had sold his soul to the cook,” growing “older and fatter” in the basement kitchen. The narrator adds that “he was very glad. He loved the basement.” Choice D sums this up: Hamlet has happily given his attention to the cook and the kitchen.

A.why_wrong: The text says Hamlet “did not mind” and “was very glad,” so he is not unhappy.

B.why_wrong: Hamlet is fatter because of the cook, but the text says he went to the basement after Jeremy left, not that he was sent there as a punishment.

C.why_wrong: The text says Hamlet “loved the basement”; nothing suggests he is waiting for Jeremy’s return.

items.passage:
The following text is from Jean Ingelow’s 1869 novel Mopsa the Fairy. Jack, a boy, has discovered a nest of miniature fairies inside a hollow tree.

Jack was very much astonished, but he went on eating his cake, and was so delighted to see the young fairy climb up the side of the hollow and scramble again into her nest, that he laughed heartily; upon which all the nestlings popped up their heads, and, showing their pretty white teeth, pointed at the slice of cake.

“Well,” said Jack, “I may have to stay inside here for a long time, and I have nothing to eat but this cake; however, your mouths are very small, so you shall have a piece;” and he broke off a small piece, and put it into the nest, climbing up to see them eat it.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
options: Jack is so frightened by the fairies that he drops his cake and tries to climb out of the tree.
Jack is delighted by the young fairies and kindly shares his cake with them.
Jack offers the fairies some cake so that they will show him the way out of the tree.
Jack is annoyed when the fairies try to take his cake, since it is the only food he has.
items.explanation: Jack is “so delighted” by the young fairy that he “laughed heartily,” and when the fairies point at his cake he says, “you shall have a piece,” and puts some into the nest. Choice B states both his delight and his kindness.

A.why_wrong: Jack is “astonished,” but he keeps eating, laughs, and climbs up to watch the fairies; he is not frightened and does not drop his cake.

C.why_wrong: Jack expects that he “may have to stay inside here for a long time” and shares the cake anyway; he does not ask the fairies for a way out.

D.why_wrong: Jack does say the cake is all he has to eat, but he gives the fairies a piece willingly because “your mouths are very small”; he is not annoyed.

items.passage:
The following text is from Barry Pain’s 1900 novel Eliza. The narrator, an office employee, recalls a conversation with a junior colleague.

“Suppose,” I said to one of the junior clerks at our office the other day, “you were asked to describe yourself in a few words, could you do it?”

His answer that he could describe me in two was no answer at all. Also the two words were not a description, and were so offensive that I did not continue the conversation.

I believe there are but few people who could give you an accurate description of themselves.
items.stem: Based on the text, how does the junior clerk most likely feel about the narrator?
options: He admires the narrator and hopes to learn from him.
He is nervous about speaking to someone more senior than himself.
He has a low opinion of the narrator.
He shares the narrator’s interest in describing people accurately.
items.explanation: When the narrator asks the clerk to describe himself, the clerk says instead that “he could describe me in two” words, and those words were “so offensive” that the narrator ended the conversation. A clerk who answers this way most likely has a low opinion of the narrator.

A.why_wrong: The clerk answers with two offensive words about the narrator, which shows no admiration.

B.why_wrong: Far from seeming nervous, the clerk boldly insults the narrator.

D.recipe: twisted detail (narrator’s interest given to the clerk)
D.why_wrong: It is the narrator who cares about accurate descriptions; the clerk’s two words “were not a description” at all.
